title: How to send and receive euros in the UK
summary: How to send and receive euros in the UK without losing money to fees. Compare SEPA, SWIFT and euro accounts, and the cheapest routes. Compare now.
body_markdown:
A UK-based freelancer receiving payments from European clients through a UK bank must receive the payment via international wire transfer. With deductions from intermediary banks and forced conversion to GBP, what should have been £1,000 ends up being less than £950. The final amount will be different if the freelancer uses a multi-currency account.


To send and receive euros in the UK, you can use a UK bank on the SWIFT or SEPA network, or a multi-currency account that gives you a euro IBAN. Receiving into a euro balance avoids forced conversion, and you convert to pounds later at the real exchange rate when it suits you.


Whether you are a UK-based freelancer invoicing European clients, receiving family support from the eurozone, or need to send euros abroad for whatever reason, understanding your options and how each works can help you reduce losses and save time. This guide clearly shows you how to receive euros and send euros using various options.


## Why euro transfers in the UK cost more than they should


In many cases, the cost of sending or receiving euros exceeds the displayed transfer fee, if it is disclosed at all. The biggest losses on each transaction usually come from undisclosed exchange rate margins, intermediary bank charges, and being forced to convert euros into pounds when you receive them.


### **The GBP/EUR conversion margin**


When a bank converts euros to pounds or pounds to euros, it uses an exchange rate that includes a margin above the real, mid-market rate. The mid-market rate is the official exchange rate you find on Google or Xe. Banks usually include a 1% to 4% margin, depending on the bank and transaction size.


This margin is almost never disclosed. It's hidden in the displayed rate. And sometimes platforms claim to charge zero transfer fees, but you end up getting 3% less due to a hidden exchange-rate margin. Comparing how much you end up with at the end of the day is a better way to compare platforms, and not just the disclosed transfer fee.


### **Fees on international transfers**


When a payment is sent through SWIFT, the sending bank, intermediary banks and receiving bank may each charge fees.


The sending bank charges the sender’s balance, not the sent amount. As the money moves from one bank to another, correspondent banks charge an undisclosed handling fee from the transferred amount. And when the money lands in the receiver’s account, some banks also charge a fee before applying the marked-up exchange rate.


These deductions can significantly reduce the final amount received. So, if an international client sends you €1,000, you might end up with €920 to €950 worth of GBP once the exchange rate is applied.


On the other hand, if you have an EUR account in the UK, EUR payments go through SEPA and not SWIFT. SEPA is the Eurozone's local payment system. So, sending and receiving EUR looks more like a domestic transfer, without international wire fees and intermediary banks. You can also hold EUR in this account and convert to GBP whenever you like. The fees are more predictable as there are no hidden fees. Conversions are usually close to the mid-market rate.


### **Forced conversion on receipt**


Many UK banks automatically convert incoming euros to pounds. This conversion usually happens at the bank’s rate, whether or not that is the best time for you to convert. If you plan to spend or hold euros again soon, being forced to convert immediately and then convert back later means paying the conversion margin twice.


Understanding the difference between SEPA and SWIFT helps you decide whether to send and receive euros in the UK. Being able to hold euros rather than being forced to convert makes a significant difference to the overall cost.


## How to receive euros into a UK account


Many UK banks can receive euro payments, but what happens after the money arrives depends on the account. Some accounts may convert incoming euros into pounds, while others offer separate foreign-currency or euro accounts. Fees and exchange rates also vary between banks. If the sender uses SWIFT rather than SEPA, correspondent bank deductions may also reduce the amount that arrives.


Instead of receiving euros into a GBP account, a dedicated euro account with its own IBAN (International Bank Account Number) lets you receive and hold euros without automatic conversion. This way, you control the EUR-to-GBP conversion and can see the rate before you confirm.


The sender just needs your account number, IBAN, and other required payment details to pay you in euros. Senders within the eurozone pay via SEPA, which is significantly cheaper and faster than a SWIFT transfer.


## How to send euros to the eurozone.


You can send euros using SEPA or an international wire (SWIFT)


### Sending euros with SEPA


[SEPA](https://www.ecb.europa.eu/) is designed for euro payments between the 36 participating countries, making cross-border euro transfers work much like domestic payments. Standard SEPA Credit Transfers generally arrive within one banking business day, while SEPA Instant can arrive within seconds when the banks involved support it.


### Sending EUR with an international wire (SWIFT)


When you send money directly from your GBP account to an account in the Eurozone, the transfer typically goes through SWIFT. The money and payment instructions go through several banks, each charging its own fees. This is why this option can be more expensive for small, frequent transfers and may take up to 5 days to complete.


### Choosing between SEPA and SWIFT


SEPA transfers are usually completed within one business day, and sometimes instantly with SEPA Instant. SWIFT transfers can take one to five business days, depending on the number of correspondent banks involved in the routing chain. So, if you are pressed for time, SEPA might be a better option.


SWIFT remains a reliable option for official transactions that need proper documentation and large sum transfers. The total cost might not seem significant for infrequent, high-value transactions.

## Frequently asked questions about sending and receiving euros in the UK


### **Can I receive euros in the UK?**


Yes. You can receive euros into eligible UK bank accounts and dedicated euro accounts. However, most accounts may automatically convert incoming euros into pounds. A dedicated euro account with an IBAN lets you hold the euros and decide when to convert them.


### **What is a euro IBAN?**


A euro IBAN is an International Bank Account Number used to identify an account for euro payments. It can be used to receive eligible payments through SEPA and provides the account details a sender needs to make a euro transfer.


### **Is SEPA cheaper than SWIFT?**


Generally, SEPA transfers are cheaper than SWIFT transfers when both are available for the same euro payment. SEPA is designed for euro payments within the SEPA area, while SWIFT is an international messaging network commonly used for payments that cross different payment networks. The actual cost depends on the banks and providers involved.


### **How do I convert euros to pounds cheaply?**


Compare the total cost, not just the advertised transfer fee. Look for a provider that uses a competitive exchange rate and clearly discloses its conversion fee. Holding euros in a euro account until you are ready to convert can also prevent unnecessary conversions.
